Tax Incidence

Who bears the burden of taxes
“Our new Constitution is now established, and has an appearance 
that promises permanency; but in this world nothing can be said to 
be certain, except death and taxes.”
—Benjamin Franklin, in a letter to Jean-Baptiste Le Roy, 1789

Who bears the burden of taxes
Question: who pays the tax?
• Seem to be a stupid question? Whoever is taxed 
bears the burden.

Tax Incidence
This answer might be too naive
• We are going to see that the tax burden can be shared 
between a buyer and a seller even if it seems to fall on 
just one of them. 
• We will use a term tax incidence to denote this situation
• Tax incidence: how the burden of the tax is distributed 
across various agents in the economy.

An example
Suppose the government of Hangzhou wants to raise money 
to build a few additional toilets near Xihu, because the 
number of toilets there is quite limited for quite a few years.
• Knowing that the restaurants near Xihu are doing well, 
government decides to levy a tax of 2RMB on every dish of 
Xihu Vinegar Fish (西湖醋鱼)
• Every time a restaurant sells a dish of fish it must send 2 
RMB to the city tax department.

An example
Question: 
• How is this going to affect price and quantity
of Vinegar fish sold in Hangzhou?
• How is this going to affect sellers and buyers in 
the market?
An example

• Now, there is a gap of 2 RMB between what the consumer 
pays and what the supplier receives
• Second, not all of this 2RMB falls on the restaurants: 
• Consumers are paying 1RMB more per plate
• Sellers are receiving 1RMB less per plate
An example

Suppose now the sellers begin to complain as they 
are unhappy with paying the 2 RMB tax. 
• Here is their argument, which seem clever enough: 
“Because most of our buyers are tourists, let’s tax these 
buyers 2 Yuan for every dish that they purchase. This 
way, the tourists will pay for their new toilets.” 
An example

Question:
What would happen if the government follow the
sellers’ suggestions and levied the tax on consumers
instead?
An example

Why doesn’t it change? 
• It’s because in the first case, when restaurants are taxed, 
menu prices rose from 6.50 to 7.50. 
• Thus, consumers paid 7.50 per plate and producers’ net revenue was 
5.50 (7.50 - 2 tax) per plate. 
• In the second case, when consumers are directly taxed, the 
equilibrium menu price decreases to 5.50 because of the 
consequences of the tax. 
• Thus, again, producers receive 5.50 per plate in net revenues, but, 
because of the tax, consumers pay a total of 7.50 for every dish of 
fish they consume.

A general lesson
“In competitive markets, tax incidence and equilibrium 
prices and quantities are independent of whether the 
tax is imposed on consumers or producers.”

The Effects of Demand and Supply Elasticities
• In general, the tax incidents will not be identical for
sellers and buyers, as the elasticity of market demand 
will not be identical to the elasticity of market supply.
The Effects of Supply Elasticities
The Effects of Demand Elasticities

General lesson:
The tax burden falls less heavily on the side of the 
market that is more elastic—that is, more responsive 
to price changes. 
The Effects of Demand and Supply Elasticities

What is the intuition?
• When buyers are more price-elastic, they have more 
alternatives: when the price rises, switch to another good. 
• If buyers are price inelastic, they have few good alternatives. 
• Thus, they must “swallow” the higher price and continue to 
purchase the taxed good despite the higher price. 
• Same logic applies to the producer side.

Another impact of elasticities on the tax burden: 
• As supply or demand becomes more price-elastic, 
the deadweight loss of taxation increases.
